scenario.title: Lakeside Water — billing dispute surge (Mock #6, not an official contest problem)
scenario.description: Billing dispute tickets roughly doubled in August-September. Customer Service wants an AI agent. Field reading is contracted out; AMI meters and the meter data management system (MDMS) are run by a vendor.
scenario.initial_request: Dispute tickets doubled since August. Build an AI agent that auto-answers billing dispute tickets and fixes whatever is causing the wrong bills.

potential_bias: frames the issue as a response-speed problem

CL-01.statement: Dispute tickets doubled since August. Build an AI agent that auto-answers billing dispute tickets and fixes whatever is causing the wrong bills.

H-REQUESTER-FRAME.statement: Requester believes the surge in dispute tickets is due to unknown billing errors causing wrong bills, and proposes an AI agent to auto-answer tickets and fix the underlying cause.

H-AMI-READ-GAP.statement: AMI read events are delayed or missing, leading to estimate substitution and incorrect bills, driving dispute increase.

H-FIELD-READ-DELAY.statement: Manual meter reads from field are uploaded late or incomplete, causing billing estimates and customer disputes.

H-RULE-CHANGE-IMPACT.statement: Recent changes to billing import validation rules (DA-RULES) introduced errors that produce incorrect bills.

interpretation_history.interpretation: The observation shows that disputed bills are more frequently associated with actual meter reads than estimated reads, indicating that the dispute surge is not solely driven by estimate substitution.
Field route completion is 0.88, below the 0.95 target, indicating incomplete/delayed manual meter reads that can lead to estimate substitution and incorrect bills, contributing to the dispute surge.
No tariff changes were recorded, indicating that tariff modifications are not a source of the billing dispute increase.
The dispute ticket volume rose from ~600 per month in June‑July to ~1,200 per month in August‑September, indicating a clear increase that began in August.

The observation shows dispute response times are within SLA (median 1.6 days, p90 2.8 days vs SLA 3 days) despite high ticket volume, indicating that response speed is not a contributing factor to the dispute surge. Thus the surge likely stems from bill correctness issues rather than delayed responses.
